title-group.article-title: Stochastic Economic Dispatch of a Power System With Solar Farm Considering Generation Flexibility and Reliability

license.license-p: This is an open access article distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution License, which permits unrestricted use, distribution, and reproduction in any medium, provided the original work is properly cited.

abstract.p: In this paper, a novel approach is presented for optimizing economic dispatch (ED) in power systems featuring solar farms and flexible loads. The ED problem is formulated as a multiobjective optimization task with stochastic characteristics. To address this challenge, a hybrid multiobjective algorithm named hybrid differential evolution algorithm (hDE)-multiobjective flower pollination algorithm (MOFPA) is proposed, which integrates principles from the differential evolution algorithm and the MOFPA, yielding enhanced performance. Two weighted objective functions are introduced to represent operation cost and the power system generation flexibility index (GFI) based on carefully selected scenarios. The occurrence probability of each scenario influences the objective function’s final value. Monte Carlo simulation (MCS) is utilized for scenario selection, enabling a comprehensive assessment of system performance. We first evaluate the proposed algorithm by optimizing standard benchmark functions and comparing results against those of other state-of-the-art algorithms. The outcomes demonstrate the superior accuracy and efficiency of the hDE-MOFPA algorithm. In the subsequent simulation phase, we optimally solve the ED problem, considering uncertainties and the involvement of flexible loads. A sensitivity analysis is conducted to examine the impact of uncertainties and flexible loads on both cost and emissions. The results reveal that the combined uncertainty of load and photovoltaic (PV) significantly influences the system. By adopting this novel approach, our proposed method offers valuable insights into optimizing the ED problem in power systems with solar farms and flexible loads, considering uncertainties and various scenarios. The sensitivity analysis indicates that considering uncertainties leads to a 4.9% increase in operational expenditures and a 4.1% decrease in GFI. Also, uncertainties in load and irradiation range from 5% to 20%, GFI experiences a decline from 4.08% to 20.18%, while costs undergo an increase from 4.92% to 18.93%.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Economic dispatch (ED) plays a critical role in the operation of power systems by determining the optimal operating point for generation units to minimize operation costs [1–3]. The integration of renewable energy sources, such as solar farms, introduces complexity to the ED problem due to their intermittent and uncertain nature [4, 5]. Furthermore, the considering demand response programs (DRPs), adds additional uncertainties and constraints, further complicating the issue [6]. To address these challenges, various approaches have been proposed for ED with solar farms. These approaches aim to optimize the dispatch of generation companies (GenCos) while considering operational constraints and system uncertainties [7]. Advanced optimization techniques, such as stochastic programing [8], robust optimization [9], and chance-constrained programing [10], are often employed to account for the uncertainties and risks associated with photovoltaic (PV) power and loads. Additionally, machine learning [11, 12] and artificial intelligence techniques [13–15] can be utilized to improve the accuracy and reliability of PV power and load demand forecasts.

Probabilistic modeling is applied in stochastic programing methods to incorporate uncertainties into the ED optimization problem. This approach is widely utilized in the context of PV power and loads as it effectively captures the inherent randomness associated with these factors [16]. The accuracy of stochastic models heavily relies on the quality of input data, which may introduce errors or inaccuracies, impacting the reliability of the optimization results. A study conducted in [17] demonstrates the effectiveness of stochastic programing in reducing operational costs and improving system reliability compared to deterministic and probabilistic approaches. Stochastic programing methods, while effective in capturing uncertainties through probabilistic modeling, may suffer from computational complexity, particularly when dealing with large-scale power systems. On the other hand, robust optimization provides a more conservative and reliable solution but may result in higher operating costs [18]. In Bai et al.’s [19] study, robust optimization approaches are explored, focusing on the worst-case scenario of uncertainties in ED with PV power to evaluate the tradeoff between system performance and robustness. Simulation results indicate an increase in the cost of ED. Robust optimization approaches tend to yield conservative solutions, potentially leading to higher operating costs compared to other methods. In Yang et al.’s [20] study, the effectiveness of chance-constrained programing in reducing generation costs while maintaining a specified level of reliability in ED with PV power is demonstrated. Chance-constrained programing sets a probability threshold for constraints to ensure a desired level of system reliability. This approach strikes a balance between stochastic programing and robust optimization, allowing for a tradeoff between cost and reliability. However, determining appropriate probability thresholds can be challenging and may require significant computational resources. Moreover, this method may not fully capture the complexity of uncertainties, potentially leading to underestimation or overestimation of risks associated with ED decisions.

In recent years, the application of machine learning has gained significant attention in addressing problems characterized by uncertainties. Machine learning leverages historical data and statistical models to make more accurate predictions for PV power and load demand. These predictions offer valuable insights into the patterns and behavior of these variables, thereby enhancing the precision of optimization models. Several studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of machine learning techniques, such as neural networks and support vector regression, in forecasting PV power and load demand for ED [21, 22]. The performance of machine learning models heavily depends on the quality and quantity of available data, which may be limited or subject to noise and uncertainties. Artificial intelligence encompasses various methodologies, including whale optimization algorithm [23], gravitational search algorithm [24], and improved quantum particle swarm intelligence [25], which can be utilized to optimize power generation dispatch. This approach offers flexibility and adaptability, capturing the intricate and nonlinear relationships between different factors. In a recent work [26], an artificial rabbits optimization algorithm was introduced for solving dynamic ED problems in power systems. The proposed algorithm outperformed other state-of-the-art optimization algorithms in terms of solution quality and computational efficiency, providing valuable insights into its behavior and performance. However, these algorithms may suffer from scalability issues or difficulties in handling high-dimensional optimization problems, limiting their applicability to large-scale power systems. Moreover, the performance of artificial intelligence algorithms may vary depending on the specific problem characteristics and parameter settings, requiring careful tuning and validation. Additionally, a new real-time ED [27] is proposed for ED in power systems with wind farm, considering the uncertainties associated with wind power and load demand. The study demonstrates that the integration of energy storage systems effectively reduces pollutant emissions and enhances system stability, particularly in the context of high wind power penetration. Uncertainties associated with renewable energy sources can pose challenges for real-time decision-making and may require advanced forecasting techniques or adaptive control strategies to mitigate their impacts effectively. Another study [28] focuses on multiobjective optimization for ED in power systems with PV power. The approach employs a nondominated sorting genetic algorithm (NSGA) to optimize the tradeoff between economic cost and emissions. The findings reveal that the integration of solar farms successfully reduces pollutant emissions and improves system reliability, particularly with high PV power penetration. Moreover, a novel optimization algorithm known as the improved pelican optimization algorithm is proposed [29] for solving the optimal ED problem in power systems with multiple sources. The algorithm’s superior performance in terms of solution quality and computational efficiency provides valuable insights into its behavior and effectiveness in solving ED problems.

This article presents a comprehensive and practical ED model for power systems, considering the uncertainties and risks associated with renewable energy sources and generation flexibility. The study begins with a thorough sensitivity analysis to identify the loads that have the most significant influence on the ED of the power system. The ED problem is then tackled from a probabilistic perspective, treating the occurrence coefficients of each event as a two-objective optimization problem. Probability density functions (PDFs) and the Monte Carlo simulation (MCS) method are employed for scenario selection. To address the optimization problem, a hybrid algorithm called the hybrid differential evolution algorithm (hDE)-multiobjective flower pollination algorithm (MOFPA) is proposed. Additionally, a sensitivity analysis is conducted to evaluate the impact of the uncertainties on the cost and generation flexibility index (GFI). The main contributions of this study are as follows:•
Assessing the impact of uncertainties on the cost of operation and generation flexibility in the ED program through a comprehensive sensitivity analysis.•
Introducing a comprehensive and precise ED model that integrates DRPs in an uncertain power system with solar farms.•
Introducing a novel hybrid algorithm called hDE-MOFPA, known for its high accuracy and excellent convergence properties.

The paper is organized in the following manner: Problem formulation is performed in Section 2. In this section, the under-study power system model is initially described, followed by the presentation of system flexibility. Subsequently, the proposed objective functions and ED constraints are introduced. The introduction of the innovative hDE-MOFPA algorithm is reserved for Section 3. Section 4 offers an examination of simulation outcomes, drawing comparisons with results obtained through alternative methodologies. Lastly, the conclusions and recommendations for prospective research are provided in Section 5.

sec.title: 2. Problem Formulation
sec.p: In the past decade, there has been a decrease in the use of fossil fuels for electricity supply due to environmental problems and rising fuel prices. As a result, there has been a growing shift toward renewable energy sources such as PV, water, and wind units. However, the widespread integration of renewable resources can introduce uncertainties in power system studies. Therefore, it is crucial to develop a suitable power system model that takes into account these uncertainties for effective ED studies. Furthermore, flexibility is another crucial factor in power system studies that require special attention. Enhancing flexibility indicators within the power system can enhance its reliability and reduce operating costs. Thus, it is essential to prioritize the optimization of flexibility in power system planning and operations.

sec.title: 2.1. The Power System Model Under Uncertain Conditions
sec.p: Figure 1 illustrates the overall structure of the power system investigated under uncertain conditions. The system comprises thermal units, a hydro unit, and a solar farm. Integrating solar farms into the system has reduced overall emissions due to their clean energy production. However, the higher generation costs linked with solar farms compared to other GenCos have led to increased overall costs. Leveraging power generation from solar farms or curtailing the consumption of flexible loads can mitigate capacity constraints on GenCos, thus enhancing the GFI. The loads within the system are categorized into two groups: loads participating in the DRP and other loads. Various DRPs are available, yet this article centers on employing direct control of flexible loads and pricing strategies to attain economic and environmentally sustainable load distribution within the power system.

sec.p: In order to account for the uncertainties in the ED problem, an iterative approach can be the optimal solution. The uncertainties related to load and solar renewable farms have been incorporated into the objective functions, as shown in Equation (1):(1)OF=∑s=1NsProbs×Fs.

This strategy guarantees that the objective functions are minimized when both cost and emission levels are minimized across all selected scenarios. Notably, the inclusion of the weight factor of scenarios in the objective function means that scenarios with lower probabilities, exert a diminished influence on the final value of the objective function.

PDFs are pivotal in representing uncertainties across various parameters of power systems, including demand and renewable energy generation. MCS leverages these PDFs to generate multiple scenarios by sampling from the probability distributions. The selected scenarios encapsulate the spectrum of potential outcomes under uncertain conditions. By simulating these scenarios, MCS furnishes a comprehensive framework for evaluating the efficacy of ED strategies across diverse uncertain scenarios. This enables decision-makers to optimize ED while accounting for the inherent uncertainties in the power system, thereby bolstering the robustness and reliability of dispatch solutions.

Various dynamic elements, including seasonal variations and environmental circumstances, customer behavior, and industrial operations, play a role in the consumption uncertainties. To better capture the uncertainties related to electrical loads, a commonly used approach is the utilization of the normal PDF. The normal PDF is characterized by two key parameters: the mean (μ) and the standard deviation (σ), as shown in Equation (2) [30]:(2)Norm PDFx=12π×σe−x−μ22×σ2.

In the model proposed in this article, economic load distribution within the power system is performed with the integration of solar farms. The prediction of solar farm production power is challenging due to fluctuations in the intensity of solar radiation caused by shadow conditions. Several factors influence the production power, including the PV power curve, solar radiation intensity, radiation angle, and solar array dimensions. To estimate the solar energy potential in a region, a probability model is developed using historical data. Since solar radiation intensity is a random variable, meteorological data can serve as a suitable basis for estimation. The uncertainty linked to the probabilistic nature of solar radiation intensity is represented by utilizing the Beta PDF, as shown in Equation (3) [31]:(3)Beta PDFir=Γαsolar+βsolarΓαsolar.Γβsolarirαsolar−11−irβsolar−1,where ir represents the intensity of solar radiation, Γ denotes the gamma function, and αsolar and βsolar are the coefficients of the beta distribution function. The values of αsolar and βsolar can be determined using historical irradiation data.

In this study, the selection of scenarios is accomplished through the implementation of the MCS methodology. By employing MCS to randomly sample scenarios, a comprehensive array of potential conditions that could manifest within the power system is encompassed. This diverse assortment of scenarios facilitates the identification of the most likely circumstances [32].

sec.title: 2.2. Price Elasticity and Generation Flexibility
sec.p: Dynamic pricing involves determining the cost of electricity based on real-time supply and demand conditions, resulting in fluctuations throughout the day to reflect changing electricity requirements and availability. Despite its potential benefits, such as improved resource allocation and consumer engagement, widespread implementation has been hindered by the need for accurate information platforms [33]. In contrast, time-of-use (TOU) pricing establishes different electricity rates for different time periods. Consumers can adjust their consumption patterns to take advantage of lower rates during off-peak hours, resulting in potential cost savings. TOU pricing empowers consumers to make informed decisions about their electricity usage, leading to improved overall system efficiency. It also provides consumers with greater control over their electricity consumption based on their financial circumstances. Critical point pricing (CPP) is another pricing method where electricity prices experience a significant increase during peak hours. This method aims to manage demand in the electricity market [34]. By reducing consumption during peak periods, the strain on the electricity grid is alleviated, minimizing the need for additional power generation facilities and enhancing system efficiency. The model incorporates the concept of price elasticity of demand, which is defined below.

sec.title: 2.2.1. Price Elasticity
sec.p: The concept of demand elasticity reflects the extent to which customer demand reacts to fluctuations in product prices. In the context of a power system, statistical and mathematical analyses can be employed to model the price elasticity of demand. These models aid in predicting electricity demand within the hub and optimizing demand response initiatives. By leveraging these demand-price elasticity models, it becomes feasible to optimize energy consumption in the power system and determine an appropriate electricity price that maintains a balance between supply and demand. As demand and supply share a direct correlation in a power system, effective demand management plays a pivotal role in optimizing efficiency and reducing overall system costs. The calculation of price elasticity of demand involves assessing the sensitivity of demand to price variations. Therefore, the price elasticity during period t, in comparison to period h, can be defined as in Equation (4) [35, 36]:(4)Et,h=PhDt∂Dt∂Ph.

The E (t, h) is price elasticity represents the extent to which consumption varies in the t period due to price fluctuations in the h period. Depending on the variations in demand elasticity across different time periods, two types of elasticity can be identified: internal elasticity and cross-elasticity of demand. Internal elasticity pertains to loads that demonstrate sensitivity within a single period, with consumers unable to shift their consumption from one period to another. These loads, such as lighting loads, are referred to as nonshiftable loads. On the other hand, cross-elasticity applies to loads where consumers have the ability to shift their consumption between periods. Industrial loads are an example of such loads, exhibiting a notable and delayed response to changes in electricity prices. By employing this model, it becomes possible to analyze the impacts of electricity price variations and other factors influencing consumption while optimizing demand response initiatives.

To maximize the consumer’s profit, Equation (6) can be employed as follows:(6)dSdDt=0→dBDtdt−Pt=0→dBDtdt=Pt.

The profit function for elastic consumers in a single period can be determined by employing Equation (7), which calculates the profit based on load adjustments from D0 (t) to D (t):(7)BDt=B0t+P0tDt−D0t1+Dt−D0t2Et×D0t.
Through the derivation of the aforementioned equation and its subsequent integration into Relation (7), we can establish the following relationship:(8)Pt=P0t1+Dt−D0tEt×D0t.
Consequently, Equation (9) can be utilized to determine the collective demand quantity required to enhance profitability:(9)Dt=D0t1+EtPt−P0tPt.

sec.title: 2.2.1.3. Economic Load Model
sec.p: The economic modeling of load within the power system encompasses a combination of single-period elastic loads and multiperiod elastic loads, which can be represented by Equation (13):(13)Dt=D0t1+EtPh−P0hP0h+∑h=1,h≠t24Et,hPh−P0hP0h.

By employing the aforementioned equation, it becomes feasible to compute the consumption of consumers within the power system following the implementation of DRPs. Additionally, considering the fluctuations in energy prices within the market, it is possible to ascertain the quantity of demand for each time period.

sec.title: 2.2.2. Generation Flexibility
sec.p: Flexibility refers to the capability of a system to effectively handle modeled uncertainties within reasonable timeframes and costs. In the context of a power system, generation flexibility pertains to the system’s ability to adapt its generation capacity dynamically to accommodate evolving conditions while ensuring reliable and efficient operations. This involves leveraging different resources and technologies, such as power plant generation capacity, spinning reserves, DRPs, and renewable farms, to manage the balance between load demand and supply. Enhancing generation flexibility in the power sector through optimization can contribute to improved system resilience, reduced energy expenses, and increased integration of renewable energy sources. This is crucial for establishing a sustainable and dependable energy system capable of meeting the evolving demands of modern society. When operating a power system with n flexible generation units over a time interval of t = [1, T], the solution to the problem involves an array of power system load values. This array can be represented as a matrix, as illustrated below [37]:(14)P∗=P11∗⋯P1n∗⋮⋱⋮PT1∗⋯PTn∗.

During the analysis of flexibility, the primary goal is to assess the potential for modifying the values within the matrix arrays and to ascertain their maximum permissible variations:(15)ΔPij=Pijnew−Pij∗,where the positive and negative power variations are examined independently to assess the magnitude of positive and negative flexibility. The degree of flexibility can be evaluated by employing Equation (16):(16)fij=ΔPijPijnew.
The sum of the values in Equation (16) represents the measure of flexibility within the power system. Consequently, the GFI for a power system can be computed using Equation (17):(17)GFI=∑∀ifij.

sec.title: 2.3. Objective Functions and Constraints
sec.p: Similar to other optimization problems, it is crucial to establish accurate and comprehensive objective functions for the power system ED problem. These objective functions enable the determination of optimal capacities for decision variables by minimizing them. In this paper, the first objective function under consideration is the operating cost function, which is formulated in Equation (18). The proposed cost function encompasses various components, including the cost of thermal units, the cost of hydro units, the cost of combined heat and power (CHP) units, the cost of solar farms, the cost of participating in the DRP, and an environmental pollution penalty:(18)Min f1=Min∑k=1NSProbκ∑t=1Tcostt,k=Min∑k=1NKProbκ∑t=1TCTht,k+CDRt,k+CENSt,k+CEmissiont,k,where CTh (t, k), CDR (t, k), and CEmission (t, k) represent the power generation costs of thermal units, solar farms, the cost of participating in the DRP, and the environmental pollution penalty in the time period t. Ns denotes the number of random samples selected through MCS under various operational conditions. Additionally, in this context, Probk signifies the probability of the given scenario. The cost of power generation by thermal units is determined using Equation (19) [35]:(19)CTht,k=∑i=1NThCF−Thit,k+CSC−Thit,k,where CF-Th (t, k) represents the fuel cost of the thermal unit, and CF-Th (t, k) accounts for the shutdown and startup costs of the ith unit. The fuel supply cost for the thermal unit can be computed by considering the impact of the steam valve effect, as shown in Equation (20). The steam valve effect on the calculation of the thermal unit’s fuel cost is represented in a sinusoidal form:(20)CF−Thit=aiPi2t,k+biPit,k+ci+disineiPMini−Pit,k.

The shutdown and startup cost can be formulated using Equation (21):(21)CSC−Thit,k=SUCi× Uit,k−Uit−1,k ,where U is a binary coefficient that indicates whether the unit is shutdown or in operation. SUC represents the cost of shutdown and startup, which is calculated using Equation (22) based on the duration of the shutdown:(22)SUCi=HSCiToff≤CSTi+MDTiCSCiToff>CSTi+MDTi.

In Equation (22), HSCi refers to the hot startup cost and CSCi represents the cold startup cost of the ith unit. Additionally, Toff denotes the duration of the unit’s outage and CSTi and minimum down time (MDTi) are the required time for cold startup and the minimum time the unit is off, respectively.

The costs associated with solar farm can be calculated using Equation (23). It is important to note that a first-order model is used for the cost estimation of renewable solar farms. In this cost model, the coefficients are chosen to encompass various factors such as service and maintenance costs, array surface cleaning expenses, personnel costs, and electric energy transmission costs. Utilizing second-order or higher equations for the cost estimation of PV systems would increase the complexity of the problem without significantly impacting the final result:(23)CPVt,k=apvPpvt,k+bpv,where apv and bpv represent the cost coefficients of solar farms, while Ppv (t, k) denotes the production power of the PV farm. The loads within the power system were categorized into two groups: loads participating in the load response program and other loads. The reward to be paid by participating loads in the load response program can be calculated using Equation (24):(24)CDRt,k=PDRt,k×RDRt,where PDR (t) represents the amount of power reduction by flexible loads in the power system and RDR (t) signifies the predetermined reward for the reduction of power consumption, as determined by dispatching for each hour. It is important to note that the bonus is applicable only during peak hours, and no bonus is considered for reducing consumption during other times. In this paper, the power system operator was granted the authority to implement controlled blackouts for specific loads during certain hours in order to reduce operational costs. These blackouts are subject to a penalty. The penalty for unsupplied energy can be calculated using Equation (25):(25)CENSt,k=Pdeft,k×Rdeft,where Pdef (t, k) represents the power deficiency and Rdef (t) signifies the penalty paid for each MW/h of unsupplied electrical energy. The reason for this action is that the operator removes a portion of the load to prevent instability in the power system. The power deficiency is calculated as the sum of unwanted unsupplied power (Pdef-UW) resulting from system failures and the wanted interruption (Pdef-W) requested by the operator. For this paper simulation, the value of Pdef-UW is stochastically determined using the normal PDF:(26)Pdeft,k=Pdef−Wt,k+Pdef−UWt,k.

Finally, the pollution fine is also computed using Equation (26). It is important to note that, in the power system under study, pollution is exclusively associated with thermal units due to fossil fuel combustion. Other sources are renewable sources and do not contribute to emissions.(27)CEmissiont,k=∑i=1NThαiPi2t,k+βiPit,k+γi.

The second objective function focuses on enhancing the flexibility of the power system. By prioritizing power system flexibility, the overall reliability is improved, leading to reduced instances of blackouts and outages. The power system operator can allocate resources to maximize system flexibility. Since the multiobjective optimization algorithm simultaneously minimizes or maximizes two criteria, the second objective function is formulated, as shown in Equation (28):(28)Min f2=Min∑k=1NSProbκ∑t=1T1GFIt,k.

The operation of the power system should be optimized to minimize operating costs while maximizing flexibility. Economic load dispatch involves several constraints to ensure optimal operation, as described below [38, 39].

sec.title: 2.3.1. Power Balance Constraint
sec.p: After resolving the ED problem, it is essential to ensure that the total power generated in the power system is equal to the total power consumption for power system stability:(29)∑i=1NThPThit,k+PPVt,k=PLoadt,k+PLosst,k−PDRt,k−PENSt,k.

sec.title: 2.3.2. Power Generation Capacity Constraint
sec.p: The power generation capacity constraints for thermal units and solar farms can be expressed, as shown in Equations (30) and (31):(30)PThi−Min≤PThit≤PThi−Max,(31)PPVS−Min≤PPVst≤PPVs−Max.

sec.title: 2.3.3. Ramp Rate Constraint
sec.p: The output power of generator units cannot instantaneously increase or decrease to any value. The rate at which the power changes for the units in the system is limited by the ramp rate constraint, as shown in Equation (32):(32)MaxPlMin,Pl,t−1−DRl≤Pl,t≤MinPlMax,Pl,t−1+URl,where DRl and URl represent the reduction limit and increase limit of the slope rate, respectively.

sec.title: 2.3.4. Prohibited Area Constraint
sec.p: Each thermal power plant unit has a specific production capacity, and various factors such as steam valve performance, sudden vibration in turbine axes, and physical limitations in machine components can introduce discontinuities in the intervals of the power–cost function curve. Figure 2 illustrates the power–cost characteristic of a thermal unit with two forbidden zones.

sec.title: 2.3.5. Reliability Constraint
sec.p: In the proposed ED model, the power system operator possesses the flexibility to selectively deactivate certain loads within predefined limits. This capability is instrumental in mitigating system instability and reducing operational expenses. Penalties for load shedding are imposed for such actions, whether they stem from the operator’s discretion or arise from inadvertent equipment failures within the network. Additionally, to mitigate the risk of additional load shedding, the loss of power supply probability (LPSP) index has been integrated, which can be calculated using Equation (33). Incorporating this criterion helps to prevent excessive blackouts, which can lead to customer dissatisfaction [28]:(33)LPSP=∑t=1TPdefictt∑t=1TPLt,where Pdefict (t) represents the blackout amount considered by the operator, and PL (t) is the total amount of electrical demand in the power system. If the LPSP value exceeds 2%, significant penalties are enforced. This provision aims to incentivize the prevention of additional load shedding, thereby enhancing subscriber satisfaction through the reduction of blackout occurrences.

sec.title: 3. Proposed Optimization Algorithm
sec.p: The performance and accuracy of optimization algorithms are completely influenced by the meticulous selection of their parameters. Incorrect parameter settings can hinder the algorithm’s effectiveness and even impede convergence. Therefore, when transitioning between different types of optimization problems, it becomes imperative to recalibrate these parameters accordingly. Unfortunately, many researchers either overlook the need to adjust the algorithm’s parameters or rely on trial-and-error methods, which may not yield optimal outcomes. In this paper, to solve the ED problem in the power system and minimize its objective functions, a modified hDE-MOFPA is proposed. In the proposed hDE-MOFPA algorithm, we address this challenge through a hybrid approach. Specifically, the parameters of the MOFPA are dynamically adjusted using the differential evolution (DE) algorithm to enhance performance. This adaptive parameter tuning ensures that the algorithm can effectively adapt to different optimization problems, thus improving its overall performance and convergence properties. sec.title: 4. Analysis of Simulation Results
sec.p: This section is divided into two separate parts, each focusing on different aspects. The first section explores the effectiveness of the hDE-MOFPA algorithm by optimizing benchmark functions and conducting a comparative analysis with alternative algorithms for multiobjective optimization. The following section examines the application of the proposed approach to ED, which is further divided into three components. Within this section, the assessment of the proposed ED technique includes examining uncertainties and evaluating the impact of the DRP. The simulations were conducted using Matpower 7.1 within the MATLAB 2023b software environment, running on an Acer laptop equipped an Intel Core (TM) i5-6200U CPU @2.3 GHz 2.40 GHz and 8 GB DDR3 RAM. The studied power system conforms to standard specifications, with all requisite information readily accessible in Matpower.

sec.title: 4.1. Evaluation of the Proposed hDE-MOFPA for Performance Assessment
sec.p: Within this section, an analysis is performed to evaluate the effectiveness of the hDE-MOFPA technique in optimizing the CEC’09 benchmark functions [35]. The optimization process includes both unconstrained test functions (UFs) UF1–UF10 and constrained test functions (CFs) CF1–CF7, using the hDE-MOFPA algorithm. The resulting outcomes are then compared to various multiobjective algorithms. Performance assessment is based on the computation of the inverse generational distance (IGD). Lower values of the IGD index indicate a smaller discrepancy between the actual Pareto front values and the Pareto front obtained through the optimization algorithm. After solving UF1–UF10, the corresponding IGD values were computed and presented in Table 2.

sec.p: The decreased IGD index values observed in addressing CF problems validate the improved accuracy and well-distributed solutions attained by the proposed algorithm, setting it apart from alternative approaches. Figure 5 visually displays the Pareto fronts of the proposed algorithm in comparison to the true Pareto fronts for CF1, CF2, and CF3.

caption.p: Pareto fronts of the proposed algorithm for the CFs. CFs, constraint functions; MOFPA, multiobjective flower pollination algorithm.

sec.p: One of the strengths of the proposed algorithm is its high accuracy, characterized by its ability to avoid getting trapped in local optima. However, a notable weakness of the hDE-MOFPA algorithm is its tendency to increase optimization time.

sec.title: 4.2. The ED Results Analysis
sec.p: To perform the simulation, a standard power system consisting of 10 units and two solar farms is selected. Table 4 presents the GenCo coefficients.

caption.p: The GenCo coefficients.

fn.p: Abbreviations: CST, cold startup time; GenCo, generation company; MDT, minimum down time; MUT, minimum up time.

sec.p: The nominal capacities of the solar farms are set at 100 MW, contributing ~5% of the overall power system load. The probability of solar irradiation is estimated using the beta PDF with coefficients α = 5.4 and β = 3.6, as illustrated in Figure 6.

caption.p: The solar irradiation PDF. PDF, probability density function.

sec.p: The simulations encompassed 30 scenarios, generated through the utilization of the MCS technique, which incorporates PDFs for both demand and solar irradiation. Figure 7 provides a visual representation of the electrical demand and irradiation predictions for the 30 selected scenarios.

caption.p: The 30 selected scenarios.

sec.p: The scattering witnessed in the selected scenarios highlights the impact of unpredictability in the problem data, effectively demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed approach. The ED process consists of three phases. Initially, the ED is conducted without incorporating uncertainties and the DRP. In the second phase, uncertainties are considered in the ED process, excluding the DRP. Finally, the ED is performed, accounting for both uncertainties and the DRP.

sec.title: 4.2.1. The First Phase Results Analysis
sec.p: The initial phase entails performing the ED without taking into account uncertainties or the DRP. To solve the ED problem, the proposed hDE-MOFPA algorithm, along with the MOFPA algorithm, NSGA-II, multiobjective particle swarm optimization (MOPSO) algorithm, and multiobjective gray wolf optimization (MOGWO) algorithm are utilized. Figure 8 presents a visual depiction of the Pareto fronts obtained by these algorithms.

sec.p: According to the obtained results, the hDE-MOFPA algorithm has resulted in the lowest operating cost and the highest GFI index after solving the ED problem. The operation cost is 586,367$ and the GFI is 4.187 p.u. for the proposed hDE-MOFPA algorithm. In Figure 9, the power production capacity of each GenCo and solar farm over a 24-h period after solving the ED problem using the proposed hDE-MOFPA algorithm is depicted.

caption.p: The generation capacity of the GenCo units in the first phase of the simulation. GenCo, generation company.

sec.p: GenCo 1 and GenCo 2 contributed the largest portion of the system load. Additionally, solar farms provided ~1.9% of the load in the power system. To conduct a comprehensive assessment of the impact of solar farm penetration rate on the outcomes, a sensitivity analysis was carried out. This analysis involved examining the effects of varying the solar farm penetration rate from 5% to 20% on the costs and GFI. The results of this analysis are illustrated in Figure 10.

caption.p: Impact of increasing the penetration of solar farms on cost and GFI. GFI, generation flexibility index.

sec.p: The results in Figure 10 revealed that as the solar farm penetration rate rises, there is a noticeable decrease in operation cost and GFI improvement. The cost reduction for a 5% penetration rate of solar farms is 2.87% and the GFI improvement is 10.34% and for a 20% penetration rate, the cost reduction percentage and GFI improvement percentage are 10.45% and 1.17%, respectively.

sec.title: 4.2.2. The Second Phase Results Analysis
sec.p: In this phase of the simulation results analysis, the ED problem of the power system is tackled, considering uncertainties in both the load and renewable generation, while excluding the DRP. The ED is performed for all 30 selected scenarios of electric demand and solar irradiation. Figure 11 illustrates the Pareto fronts obtained through the optimization algorithms.

sec.p: Based on the findings, the hDE-MOFPA algorithm has delivered the most favorable outcomes in terms of minimizing operation cost and maximizing the GFI index subsequent to addressing the ED problem. The operation cost is recorded as $959,843, while the GFI stands at 3.679 p.u. for the proposed hDE-MOFPA algorithm. The results indicate that accounting for uncertainties has resulted in an upward trend in operational costs while concurrently diminishing the GFI. Considering uncertainties in ED analyses contributes to a 4.9% upsurge in operational expenditures and a 4.1% reduction in the GFI. Figure 12 provides a graphical representation of the power generation capacity of each GenCo and solar farm throughout a 24-h period following the resolution of the ED problem using the proposed hDE-MOFPA algorithm.

caption.p: The generation capacity of the GenCo units in the second phase of the simulation. GenCo, generation company.

sec.p: Continuing with the analysis of the simulation results in this phase, the influence of uncertainties on the cost increase and flexibility index decrease of the power system has been evaluated. The impact of uncertainties on the operation cost and GFI is depicted in Figure 13.

caption.p: Impact of load and irradiation uncertainties on cost and GFI. GFI, generation flexibility index.

sec.p: Based on the results, it has been observed that uncertainties contribute to an increase in operating costs and a decrease in the GFI. However, it is crucial to consider uncertainties in a manner that ensures the increase in costs remains reasonable and realistic. Incorporating uncertainties with low probabilities of occurrence may result in an excessive rise in operational costs or overlook operational constraints. The simultaneous uncertainty of load and irradiation has the most significant impact on costs and GFI within the power system. As the uncertainties in load and irradiation increase from 5% to 20%, the GFI decreases from 4.08% to 20.18%, while the cost increases from 4.92% to 18.93%.

sec.title: 4.2.3. The Third Phase Result Analysis
sec.p: For the third phase of the simulation result analysis, the DRP and also uncertainties are considered in the ED problem. The Pareto front obtained from the application of multiobjective optimization algorithms for this phase is illustrated in Figure 14.

sec.p: The results show that considering DRP in the ED problem results in a 1.02% cost reduction and a 2.76% increase in GFI.

sec.title: 5. Conclusion
sec.p: This study introduces a novel approach for optimizing ED and emission dispatch in a power system that incorporates solar farms and flexible loads. The ED problem is formulated as a stochastic multiobjective optimization problem, and a hybrid heuristic algorithm named hDE-MOFPA is proposed to tackle it. The hDE-MOFPA algorithm combines the DE algorithm with MOFPA. To address the multiobjective nature of the problem, two weighted objective functions are defined that capture the operation cost and emission based on selected scenarios. The probability of occurrence for each scenario influences the contribution of the corresponding objective function to the final value. The MCS method is employed to select these scenarios. The simulations are conducted in two phases. In the first phase, the performance of the proposed algorithm is evaluated by optimizing standard benchmark functions and comparing the results with those of other algorithms. The outcomes of this phase demonstrate the superior accuracy of the hDE-MOFPA algorithm compared to alternative optimization algorithms. In the second phase, the ED problem is solved optimally, considering uncertainties and the involvement of flexible loads, as well as without considering them. Additionally, a sensitivity analysis is performed to examine the effects of uncertainties in flexible loads on cost and emission. The findings reveal that considering uncertainties leads to an increase in operational costs and a decrease in the GFI. Accounting for uncertainties in ED analyses leads to a 4.9% rise in operational expenditures and a 4.1% decrease in the GFI. Incorporating uncertainties with low probabilities of occurrence can potentially lead to a disproportionate increase in operational costs or neglect of operational constraints. The combined uncertainty of load and irradiation has the most significant impact on costs and the GFI within the power system. As the uncertainties in load and irradiation range from 5% to 20%, the GFI experiences a decline from 4.08% to 20.18%, while the cost undergoes an increase from 4.92% to 18.93%. Future research could explore the development of advanced optimization techniques capable of accommodating complex uncertainties and dynamic operational conditions more comprehensively. Additionally, further investigation into the integration of renewable energy sources, DRPs, and emerging technologies such as energy storage systems and smart grids is warranted. By tackling these challenges, future research endeavors can contribute to the development of more robust and efficient ED strategies tailored for modern power systems. In future research, exploring the integration of storage systems, such as electric vehicle parking lots located alongside solar farms, can be considered to assess their influence on studies related to ED.
